newsitem.title: INDIA: India ruling coalition hopes for crisis solution.
newsitem.headline: India ruling coalition hopes for crisis solution.

text.p: India's ruling United Front coalition said on Monday it still hoped for a solution to the country's political crisis, but the rebellious Congress party reaffirmed a vow to bring down Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government.

The United Front's highest decision-making body will meet on April 9 to discuss the political situation and seek ways to approve the ground-breaking 1997/98 budget in parliament, party spokesman Jaipal Reddy said.
It will try to engineer consensus on the budget in consultation with the speaker of the lower house of parliament and other political parties, Reddy added.
The coalition faces a confidence vote in the lower house on Friday, called by President Shankar Dayal Sharma after Congress president Sitaram Kesri withdrew his party's make-or-break support.
"We are having informal talks with Congress. We are not ruling out formal talks when the stage is set," Reddy told a briefing.
"I think as and when outlines of an accord between the Congress and United Front emerge, formal talks can be held as well," he said, adding he hoped for a solution.
But Congress stuck to its guns and pledged to bring down Deve Gowda's 10-month-old minority government.

"It is highly unlikely that anything will happen before (Friday)," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said when asked what his party's next steps would be. "Let the government fall first and then we will decide."
"Negotiations are continuing at various levels. But there is no breakthrough," Gadgil later said.

Meanwhile news agencies quoted leaders of the pro-separatist sikh party Akali Dal, a key ally of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as saying it has pledged to support Deve Gowda in the confidence vote.

They said leaders of the Akali Dal, which has eight seats in the lower house, met Deve Gowda and said it would help the United Front government to fight against the Congress as it was opposed to elections at this stage.
The United Front, whose members range from free traders to communists, has needed the support of 140 Congress lawmakers in the 545-seat lower house of the parliament for its survival.
The United Front has 180 deputies in the house, which currently has 542 sitting members.
Congress president Kesri on Sunday made a strong attack on Deve Gowda, threatening to scuttle informal talks between some United Front and Congress leaders to resolve the crisis.
"Deve Gowda should go," Gadgil said.
Kesri's attack is seen as an attempt to split the 15-party government and woo some regional parties from the coalition over to Congress.
"They (Congress) made a disastrous miscalculation and want us (United Front) to pay the price," United Front spokesman Reddy told Reuters earlier on Monday.
The United Front stood solidly behind Deve Gowda, Reddy said, adding that Kesri's attack on Deve Gowda would boomerang.
"Congress will break up before April 10," he predicted.
Many politicians feel the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), the largest in the lower house with 162 members, will be the only gainer from the impasse.
"The party's intention is to vote out the government. It is not interested in a change of leadership in the United Front," The Times of India newspaper quoted BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj as saying.
BJP party secretary Venkiah Naidu told Reuters,"We are keeping our options open (on the claim to form the government)."
